name: Tooth sharpening / filing

image.caption: PSM V39 D509 Malaysian examples of tooth filing

lead: Tooth sharpening or filing is the deliberate reshaping of tooth edges, most often giving canines or incisors a pointed or flattened shape. It has a long history as a beauty, status and coming-of-age practice in several cultures.
People who do it today treat it as body modification: the smile gets a distinctive sharp or fanged look. Because the shaping removes enamel, the result is permanent.

paras: Traditional practitioners use hand tools such as chisels and files, while modern versions are done with dental instruments. Because it permanently removes tooth structure, anyone considering it is generally pointed to a licensed dentist rather than home methods.

Enamel does not regenerate, and removing it can expose the softer dentin beneath, which is more prone to wear and sensitivity. Traditional filings done without anaesthetic involve pain, and unsterile tools carry infection risk.

chain: Enamel at the tooth edge is filed
Teeth take a pointed or reshaped form
angle.text: The filing changes the shape of the tooth edge immediately, producing a pointed or flattened smile. The look is a deliberate style choice and permanent.

lead: Tooth sharpening, also called tooth filing, is a form of dental modification in which the tips or edges of teeth are filed into points or other shapes [1]. It has been recorded in Africa, Indonesia and Mesoamerica, where it signified beauty, adulthood or rank [1].
Today it is mostly an aesthetic body modification, giving the smile a pointed or fang-like look [1].
infobox: Herero, Mentawai, Bali, Congo groups, Mesoamerica

paras: Examples include Herero adolescents around 1910 who had upper teeth filed into V-shapes as a mark of beauty, men and women in the Upoto of the central Congo who filed teeth, and prehistoric and 17th-century Indonesian communities in Java, Bali and Flores, where filing was associated with nobility [1]. In Bali, the potong gigi ceremony files the canines of teenagers as a rite of adulthood, believed to remove anger and jealousy [1]. In Mentawai, sharpening tied to puberty and beliefs about the soul and is practised with a chisel without anaesthetic [1].
Contemporary filing is chosen for appearance and as body modification, and practitioners include performers such as the circus artist Horace Ridler [1].

Enamel has no blood vessels or nerves and cannot regenerate; damage beyond remineralisation cannot be repaired by the body or restored by dentists. Beneath it lies dentin, which is less mineralised, and enamel without dentin support is prone to fracture, so removal exposes deeper tissue [2].
